result.summary: A set of short fragments from Hesiod's Catalogue of Women trace the descendants of Deucalion and Hellen, including Graecus, Macedon, Magnes and the Aeolid line. Others give tales of Bellerophon and Pegasus, Endymion, the sons of Actor and Molione, the shape-shifter Periclymenus, and Nestor's escape from Heracles.

scenes.title: Descendants of Deucalion and Hellen
scenes.summary: Scholars report Hesiod's genealogy: Deucalion's line, Pandora's son Graecus, Thyia's sons Magnes and Macedon, and Hellen's sons and grandsons who ruled Thessaly.

scenes.title: The Aloiadae
scenes.summary: The Aloiadae are said to be sons of Poseidon and Iphimedea, called after Aloeus, who founded Alus.

scenes.title: Eurynome and Bellerophon
scenes.summary: Glaucus woos the wise Eurynome, but Zeus decrees his children will not be his own. Poseidon fathers Bellerophon, who rides Pegasus and kills the Chimera.
scenes.stakes: Glaucus's hope of fathering his own children is thwarted by Zeus's decree.

scenes.title: Endymion and the Molionidae
scenes.summary: Endymion receives from Zeus the choice of when to die. The sons of Actor and Molione are really sons of Poseidon.

scenes.title: Twin Bodies Joined
scenes.summary: Porphyrius says Hesiod made the twins double-bodied and joined together.

scenes.title: Periclymenus the Shape-shifter
scenes.summary: Periclymenus, gifted by Poseidon with many shapes, attacks Heracles and is shot through Athene's scheme.
scenes.stakes: Periclymenus faces mortal wounding by Heracles.

scenes.title: Nestor and Polycaste
scenes.summary: Heracles kills eleven sons of Neleus, but Nestor survives at Gerenon. Nestor's daughter Polycaste bears Persepolis to Telemachus.
scenes.stakes: Nestor's survival while his brothers are slain.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet and variant spelling for the goddess Athena.

notable_quotes.reason: Brief mention of Bellerophon slaying the Chimera with Pegasus.
Vivid list of Periclymenus's shape-shifting forms.

analysis.text: The fragments show the Catalogue's aim: tracing heroic families from gods and ancestors, linking peoples and regions to a common descent.
Genealogies like these explained ethnic names such as Greeks, Macedonians and Magnesians, and are known only through quotations by later scholars.

legacy.text: Hesiodic genealogy of Hellen and his sons Dorus, Xuthus and Aeolus underlies the Greek idea of the Dorian, Aeolian and Ionian peoples.

fun_facts.text: These fragments survive only as quotations in later writers and on papyri such as Oxyrhynchus 421, so many lines are broken.

language_notes.text: A scholiast is an ancient commentator whose notes in manuscript margins preserve fragments of lost works like Hesiod's Catalogue.
"Lacuna" marks a gap where the source text is missing or lost.
Pallas Athene is the goddess of wisdom and crafts; she is credited with teaching Eurynome her skills.
"Drove oxen for her" refers to bride-gifts: the suitor offered cattle to the woman's family as a bridal payment.
"Bent his head in oath" means Zeus swore by nodding, his usual sign of binding assent.
Pegasus is the winged horse that Bellerophon rides in his adventures.
Endymion's gift from Zeus is to choose the time of his death; later tradition links him with eternal sleep.
The Dioscuri are Castor and Polydeuces, ordinary twins with separate bodies, contrasted here with the joined Molionidae.
The yoke-boss is the knob at the centre of a chariot yoke.

context_notes.text: The Latin/Greek naming story ties peoples' names to mythic brothers, a common ancient way to explain ethnic origins.
These sons of Aeolus are ancestors of famous heroic families, including Jason's line through Cretheus and Odysseus's line through Sisyphus.
The Aloiadae (Otus and Ephialtes) are giants of myth; having a divine father while bearing a mortal's name is a typical genealogical doubling.
Bellerophon is thus the son of Poseidon, though raised in Glaucus's house as his mortal son.
Nestor, king of Pylos, survives the slaughter of his brothers by Heracles and later appears in the Iliad as an aged counsellor.

literary_notes.text: Scent from her clothes and beauty "wafted" from her eyes exaggerate her allure into something almost physical and divine.
The audience is told that Glaucus's courtship is doomed by Zeus's will, while Glaucus himself is unaware.
Pegasus is compared to the gales, conveying his tireless speed.
The list of Periclymenus's transformations, from eagle to ant to bees to snake, shows the epic fondness for enumeration and marvel.
The very gifts that made Periclymenus powerful become the means of his undoing.
